# Copy frameworks for LinkedIn messages and cold email: origin, shape, fit, evidence

Research pass of 2026-10-29. Scope: every copywriting framework a LinkedIn invitation note, first message or
follow-up (and a cold email) can borrow, traced to its author where a trace exists, with an example of each in
English and French, and the evidence behind it. It builds on, and does not repeat, `../linkedin-messages/`
(what the data says about notes, length, asks, sequences), `../cold-email/` (the practitioner email structures:
Holland, Braun, Bay, Michael, Ross, Berman) and `../personas/` (Schwartz as a persona field).

Files: `evidence.md` (every claim, its source, its rating), `sources.md` (every URL and whether it was read in
full). Ratings used everywhere: **measured** (study or large dataset with a stated method), **survey**
(self-reported), **practice** (experienced practitioners, nobody measured it), **vendor** (a seller's own data),
**untraced** (repeated, no source found, or the source does not say it).

Three books were read in their own text, not through summaries: Schwartz, *Breakthrough Advertising* (1966),
chapters 2 and 3; Caples, *Tested Advertising Methods* (fifth edition, revised by Fred E. Hahn, 1997), including
David Ogilvy's foreword to the fourth edition; and the full results table of O'Keefe and Hoeken (2021). Everything
else is marked where only a summary was reachable.

---

## 0. Summary table

| Framework | Parts | Author and origin (traced?) | Fits best | Evidence that it works |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| AIDA | Attention, Interest, Desire, Action | Credited to E. St. Elmo Lewis 1898 via E. K. Strong (1925). A 2024 history paper finds no evidence for Lewis in 1898 and points to A. F. Sheldon and F. H. Dukesmith; the acronym itself is C. P. Russell, *Printers' Ink*, 1921 | A check that a first DM has all four jobs, not a template | Hierarchy models have little empirical support (Vakratsas and Ambler 1999, measured). None for messages |
| AIDCA | Attention, Interest, Desire, Conviction, Action | Conviction step appears in Dukesmith, *Salesmanship*, 1904 (per Wikipedia's citation, not read) | Product-aware readers who need proof | None |
| ACCA | Awareness, Comprehension, Conviction, Action | Russell Colley, DAGMAR report to the Association of National Advertisers, 1961 (summaries only) | Explaining a new category to a solution-aware reader | None for copy; DAGMAR is a goal-setting model, not a writing formula |
| PAS | Problem, Agitate, Solve | No traceable inventor. Popularised by Dan Kennedy, *The Ultimate Sales Letter* (1990). Schwartz (1966) already prescribes the same three moves for "products that solve needs" | Problem-aware readers; first DM | None for the order. Threat severity alone is a weak lever; showing that the fix works is stronger (O'Keefe and Hoeken 2021, measured) |
| PASO | PAS plus Outcome | Belinda Weaver (Copywrite Matters), 2019, as her own addition | First DM where the result is easy to picture | None |
| PASTOR | Problem, Amplify, Story and Solution, Transformation and Testimony, Offer, Response | Ray Edwards, blog post of July 2014, then *How to Write Copy That Sells* (2016) | Long copy; on LinkedIn only spread across a sequence | None |
| BAB | Before, After, Bridge | No traceable inventor | Solution-aware readers; follow-up with a customer result | None |
| FAB | Features, Advantages, Benefits | Sales-training folklore; Neil Rackham (*SPIN Selling*, 1988) measured how each lands | Product-aware readers; a reply to "what do you do?" | Rackham's call research: in large sales advantages draw objections, only benefits tied to a need the buyer stated go with wins (measured, read through summaries) |
| "So what?" test | Ask "so what?" after every claim until the answer is something the reader feels | No traceable coiner | Editing every draft | Practice |
| 4Ps / PPPP | Promise, Picture, Proof, Push (or Picture, Promise, Prove, Push) | Untraced; attributed to Henry Hoke (direct mail, 1930s) by one book note; Bob Bly teaches a version | A message carrying a case or a number | None |
| 4Us | Urgent, Unique, Ultra-specific, Useful | Michael Masterson and Bill Bonner (AWAI, 2001), written for bullets, now used for headlines | Testing a subject line, a note's first line | None |
| QUEST | Qualify, Understand, Educate, Stimulate, Transition | Michel Fortin, late 1990s, teaching at Algonquin College; expanded in *The Death of the Salesletter* (2006) | A sequence: one or two stages per message | None |
| SLAP | Stop, Look, Act, Purchase | Untraced (2010s listicles) | Cheap impulse products; not B2B outreach | None |
| Star-Story-Solution | A person, their story, the fix (plus a call to action) | Untraced. One source credits Vince James, adapted by Russell Brunson; unverified | Follow-up carrying a customer story | Narrative vs non-narrative: r = .067 (measured, small) |
| Hook-Story-Offer | Hook, Story, Offer | Russell Brunson, *DotCom Secrets* (2015), *Expert Secrets*, *Traffic Secrets* (2020) | A post or a sequence, not one DM | None |
| 1-2-3-4 | What I've got, what it does for you, who I am, what to do next | Untraced; Copyblogger article, no author named | Most-aware readers, a referral or an inbound reply | None |
| Schwartz awareness | Five stages, from most aware to completely unaware | Eugene Schwartz, *Breakthrough Advertising* (1966), chapter 2, read in full | Choosing what the opening may mention | Practice (from his mail-order results, not published) |
| Schwartz sophistication | Five stages of how many competitors spoke before you | Same book, chapter 3, read in full | Choosing claim, mechanism or identification | Practice |
| Specificity (Caples, Ogilvy) | Exact facts beat general claims | Caples (1932 onward), Ogilvy's foreword to Caples; "The more informative your advertising, the more persuasive it will be" (Ogilvy) | Every line of every message | Caples' keyed ad tests (practice with counts); precise numbers read as more confident (measured); specific recommendation r = .10 (measured) |
| Monroe's motivated sequence | Attention, Need, Satisfaction, Visualization, Action | Alan Monroe, Purdue, mid 1930s (speech textbook) | The academic ancestor of PAS and BAB | The one controlled test of an order found: no difference in attitude change, but no version beat an unrelated control text (measured, small, weak) |

## 1. The seven findings that matter for messages that get answers

1. **The order of the parts is not what persuades; the parts are.** The only controlled test of a persuasive
   sequence found (Monroe's motivated sequence, Micciche, Pryor and Butler 2000, 90 participants) found no
   difference in attitude change between the canonical order, the reversed order and a random order; the
   canonical order was only rated easier to follow. Weak evidence: no version moved attitudes more than the
   unrelated control text, so the test shows no persuasion to reorder, not that order is irrelevant. A review of more than 250 studies found little support for any
   fixed hierarchy of effects (Vakratsas and Ambler 1999). Use a framework to make sure nothing is missing and the
   message reads in a sensible order. Never claim one framework "converts better": nobody has measured that.
2. **What persuades, measured over 1,149 studies:** stronger arguments (r = .19), more evidence (r = .225), showing
   that the fix works and that the reader can do it (response efficacy r = .198, self-efficacy r = .199),
   explicit arguments over implicit ones (r = .138), a specific recommendation over a vague one (r = .10).
   Framing as gain or loss: r = .016, nothing. Narrative over plain statement: r = .067. Rhetorical questions:
   r = .059. And every one of these is small and can flip sign in a given context (O'Keefe and Hoeken 2021). So a
   message should carry one real argument with one real proof and one clear next step; the shape around it is
   secondary.
3. **"Agitate" is the weakest part of PAS.** Making the threat sound bigger (threat strength r = .10, severity
   r = .116) moves people less than showing that a response works (r = .198). Practitioners already observe that
   agitation reads as pushy in a cold DM (`../cold-email/`, Hunter survey). For LinkedIn: one clause of cost, then
   the fix and its proof. PASO and BAB, which spend their words on the outcome, match the evidence better than PAS
   as usually taught.
4. **Schwartz says a cold reader cannot be sold in the first line, only identified.** Read in his own text: for the
   "completely unaware" stage you "cannot mention price, product, function or desire"; you write "an
   identification headline", "echoing an emotion, an attitude, a dissatisfaction", and its only job is to get the
   next paragraph read. For the stage where the reader has a need but does not connect it to a product, his recipe
   is literally PAS: name the need, dramatize it, present the product as the inevitable solution. So PAS is
   Schwartz's stage-four tool, not a universal one; most cold LinkedIn readers sit at stage four or five.
5. **B2B outreach is a fifth-stage sophistication market.** Schwartz's sophistication scale: first in a market you
   state the claim; second, you enlarge it; third, you explain the mechanism; fourth, you enlarge the mechanism;
   fifth, "your market no longer believes in your advertising" and the only route left is identification with the
   prospect. A decision maker has read every "we help companies like yours grow" message. Claims and mechanisms
   ("AI-powered", "save 10 hours a week") are spent; a line that shows you understand their exact situation is not.
   This is the same conclusion the personalization data reaches (`../linkedin-messages/`, finding 2) from another
   direction.
6. **Specific beats general, and this is among the best supported rules in copywriting.** Caples' cases:
   a used car dealer's general headlines ("Better automobile values") flopped, specific cars with year and price
   brought three times as many customers "by actual count" (a newspaper ad story, not a keyed split test). Ogilvy, in his foreword to Caples: "Specifics are more believable than
   generalities." Caples: "97,482 people" sounds like a count, "nearly 100,000" sounds like a copywriter's claim.
   Lab work agrees: precise numbers are read as coming from a more confident, better informed source
   (Jerez-Fernandez, Angulo and Oppenheimer 2014), and a specific recommendation persuades more than a general one
   (r = .10). On LinkedIn: one exact, checkable fact about them, one exact fact about a result, one exact next
   step. Practitioner caution (not measured in the sources read): a precise number that turns out wrong costs more
   than a round one.
7. **Give the reader the exit.** The "but you are free" line ("no worries if not", "vous êtes libre de dire non")
   raised compliance in most contexts in a meta-analysis of 42 studies (Carpenter 2013, Communication Studies; the
   effect diminished when the decision was not made on the spot, which is the usual case for a DM) and r = .175 in
   O'Keefe and Hoeken. A preregistered re-analysis (Fillon et al. 2023, 52 experiments) found a medium effect overall but none in the seven low-risk-of-bias
   studies (g = 0.11, interval crossing zero), and low reproducibility, so treat it as small and uncertain. It costs four words, matches the interest-based ask that the outreach data
   favours (`../linkedin-messages/`, finding 5), and is the opposite of what PAS's "agitate" and Brunson-style
   urgency teach.

---

## 2. What is actually measured about structure (read this before trusting any framework)

**Hierarchy of effects (AIDA and its family).** Vakratsas and Ambler (Journal of Marketing, 1999) reviewed more
than 250 papers and found "little support for any hierarchy, in the sense of temporal sequence" of advertising
effects; they propose effects in a space (cognition, affect, experience) without a fixed order. Wikipedia's AIDA
article also cites a finding that the model is a poor predictor of actual behaviour (Bendixen, "Advertising Effects
and Effectiveness", European Journal of Marketing 27(10), 1993); its abstract is an econometric study of new car
sales in South Africa and does not mention AIDA, so that citation is untraced. Rating: measured (review, read through abstract and summaries).

**A direct test of an order.** Micciche, Pryor and Butler (Psychological Reports 86(3), 2000): three versions of the
same persuasive message (Monroe's five steps in order, reversed, random) plus a control; no difference in attitude
change; the ordered version scored higher on comprehensibility on one of four comparisons. Small (21 to 24 per
group), one campus topic (a parking fee). Note what the abstract shows: no group, ordered or not, differed from a
control group that read an unrelated message, so the persuasive text itself moved nobody; the study cannot tell
"order does not matter" apart from "this message did not work". Rating: measured (abstract and catalog record
only), weak. It is still the closest thing to a framework test found anywhere.

**What single design choices are worth.** O'Keefe and Hoeken (Frontiers in Psychology, 2021) pooled 1,149 studies
(about 280,000 participants) of 30 message variations. Median effect r about .10; the 95% prediction intervals of
almost all include zero, so the on-average-better choice can lose in a given setting, even when the setting is
specified. Selected rows (full table read):

| Variation (first option vs second) | Mean r | What it means for a LinkedIn message |
|---|---|---|
| Gain vs loss framing | .016 | "You'll save" vs "you're losing": irrelevant |
| Two-sided vs one-sided | -.002 | Mentioning a downside neither helps nor hurts on average |
| Statistical vs narrative evidence | .044 | A number or a story: both fine |
| Rhetorical questions vs statements | .059 | Opening on a question is not a lever by itself |
| Narrative vs non-narrative | .067 | Star-Story-Solution has a small edge at best |
| Threat appeal strength (strong vs weak) | .100 | Agitating harder: small |
| Recommendation specificity (specific vs general) | .101 | "Reply 'yes' and I'll send the 2-page audit" beats "let me know" |
| Conclusion included vs omitted | .102 | Say what you want them to conclude |
| Argument explicitness (explicit vs implicit) | .138 | Spell the tie out; do not leave a bare fact |
| Vividness | .150 | A concrete picture beats an abstract one |
| "But you are free" included | .175 | Give the exit |
| Argument strength (strong vs weak) | .190 | The single reason has to be a good reason |
| Response efficacy (high vs low) | .198 | Show that the fix works |
| Self-efficacy (high vs low) | .199 | Show that it is easy for them |
| Evidence amount (high vs low) | .225 | Proof, not adjectives |

Explicitness (.138) is the measured version of the recited-fact failure (`../linkedin-messages/`,
finding 1): a recited fact with no tie to why you write is an implicit argument.

**The practitioner and vendor data on cold messages** (length, asks, personalization types, sequence length) is in
`../linkedin-messages/evidence.md` and `../cold-email/evidence.md`. None of it compares frameworks.

---

## 3. One scenario for every example

All examples below use the same invented situation so the frameworks can be compared on the same facts. **Every
number in the examples is illustrative: a real message uses the sender's own, checkable figures.**

- Reader: Claire Martin, finance director at a road carrier with about 300 trucks. She posted that month-end close
  takes nine days and most of it goes on chasing carrier and fuel invoices.
- Sender: Marc, who runs a small freight-invoice audit service.
- Proof the sender actually has: a carrier of similar size; 41 duplicate or wrong invoices caught in one quarter;
  close went from nine days to six.

Invitation notes are kept to 200 characters (LinkedIn's current limit, see `../linkedin-messages/`). French uses
"vous" and the space before "?" and "!". Notes, first DMs and follow-ups are the three message types; a framework
gets the type it fits, and a type it does not fit is said so.

---

## 4. The hierarchy family: AIDA, AIDCA, ACCA, Monroe

### AIDA (Attention, Interest, Desire, Action)

**Origin, traced.** The standard story is that E. St. Elmo Lewis devised it in 1898. That story rests on E. K.
Strong's *The Psychology of Selling and Advertising* (1925), which credited Lewis with "attract attention,
maintain interest, create desire" and a later "get action". Akinori Iwamoto (Japan Marketing History Review, Vol. 3
No. 2, 2024, Kansai University) went back to primary sources and found no evidence Lewis created a prototype
around 1898; he credits Arthur Frederick Sheldon (who saw the need for the fourth step earlier) and Frank H.
Dukesmith with the decisive formulation. Read: the J-STAGE abstract (Japanese, summarised by the fetch tool). The
wording in *Printers' Ink* of 9 February 1898 was anonymous. The acronym "AIDA" itself is C. P. Russell, *Printers'
Ink*, 2 June 1921, as a memory aid. Sheldon's *Successful Selling* (1911) added Satisfaction (AIDAS). Read
through Wikipedia's AIDA article and its citations.

**Structure.** Win attention, hold interest, make them want the result, ask for one action.

**When it fits.** It was built for a print ad that does the whole job alone. A LinkedIn message is too short for
four stages of copy. Use it as a checklist: does the first line earn the second, does the message give a reason
to want something, is there exactly one action? Fits a first DM to a solution-aware reader.

**Example, first DM.**
EN: "Claire, your post on the nine-day close: the invoice chasing you described is exactly where we work. A
carrier your size found 41 wrong or duplicate invoices in one quarter with us, and closes in six days now. Would
the two-page summary of how they did it be useful?"
FR : « Claire, votre post sur la clôture en neuf jours : les relances de factures que vous décrivez, c'est
précisément notre métier. Un transporteur de votre taille a repéré avec nous 41 factures en double ou erronées en
un trimestre, et clôture désormais en six jours. Le résumé de deux pages de leur démarche vous serait-il utile ? »

**Evidence.** None for messages. The hierarchy idea itself has little empirical support (measured, section 2).

### AIDCA (adds Conviction before Action)

**Origin.** No author for the acronym. The "conviction" step is old: Dukesmith's 1904 article in *Salesmanship*
used attention, interest, desire, conviction (cited by Wikipedia, not read). Lavidge and Steiner (Journal of
Marketing, 1961) also put conviction before purchase. Untraced as a named formula.

**Structure.** AIDA with a proof step (a figure, a named peer, a guarantee) before the ask.

**When it fits.** Product-aware readers who already know you and doubt you. The conviction step is what the
evidence favours most (evidence amount r = .225).

**Example, follow-up (after a first DM went unanswered).**
EN: "Claire, one fact I left out: the 41 invoices were found on the carrier's own data, checked by their
controller, not estimated by us. Happy to show you the line-by-line if useful, no obligation."
FR : « Claire, un point que j'ai omis : les 41 factures ont été trouvées sur les données du transporteur et
vérifiées par son contrôleur de gestion, pas estimées par nous. Je peux vous montrer le détail ligne à ligne si
cela vous intéresse, sans engagement. »

**Evidence.** None for the formula; strong for its added part.

### ACCA (Awareness, Comprehension, Conviction, Action) and DAGMAR

**Origin.** Russell H. Colley, *Defining Advertising Goals for Measured Advertising Results* (DAGMAR), a report for
the Association of National Advertisers, 1961. Read through summaries only. DAGMAR is a way to set measurable
advertising goals per stage, later revised by Solomon Dutka (1995); it was not written as a copy formula.

**Structure.** Make them aware, make sure they understand, convince, ask.

**When it fits.** The "comprehension" step is its one useful addition: when the offer is unfamiliar (a new
category), explain it in one plain sentence before claiming anything. Fits a first DM to a reader who knows the
problem but has never heard that it can be solved this way.

**Example, first DM.**
EN: "Claire, most carriers check freight invoices by sampling. We check every line against the rate card and the
delivery record, so duplicates and wrong surcharges get caught before payment. For a 300-truck fleet that found 41
errors in a quarter. Worth a look at what that would mean on your volume?"
FR : « Claire, la plupart des transporteurs contrôlent leurs factures par sondage. Nous vérifions chaque ligne
contre la grille tarifaire et le bon de livraison, ce qui intercepte doublons et surcharges erronées avant
paiement. Pour une flotte de 300 camions, cela a donné 41 erreurs en un trimestre. Voulez-vous voir ce que cela
donnerait sur vos volumes ? »

**Evidence.** None for copy.

### Monroe's motivated sequence (the academic ancestor)

**Origin.** Alan H. Monroe, Purdue University, speech-communication textbooks from the mid 1930s (date given as
1935 or 1943 depending on the edition cited). Read through university course pages.

**Structure.** Attention, Need, Satisfaction, Visualization (picture the future with or without the fix), Action.
It is PAS plus BAB in one: need is the problem, satisfaction the fix, visualization the after.

**Why it is here.** It is the only sequence that has been put to a controlled test (Micciche, Pryor and Butler
2000): order made no difference to persuasion, though no version beat an unrelated control text either, so the
test is weak. That result is the best available evidence on every framework in
this file. No example: use PASO or BAB, which are its short forms.

---

## 5. The problem family: PAS, PASO, PASTOR

### PAS (Problem, Agitate, Solve or Solution)

**Origin, traced as far as it goes.** No inventor found. Dan Kennedy calls it "the most reliable sales formula ever
invented" in *The Ultimate Sales Letter* (first edition 1990, Adams Media; later editions 2000, 2006, 2011);
quoted by several secondary sources, exact wording not checked against the book. Copyblogger's 2014 article
(Demian Farnworth) says he learned it from a direct-response newsletter archive and names no inventor. **New
finding from the primary text:** Schwartz (1966, chapter 2, "How to Introduce Products That Solve Needs") gives the
same recipe in his own words: "you start by naming the need and/or its solution in your headline. Then dramatize
the need so vividly that the prospect realizes just how badly he needs the solution. And then present your
product as the inevitable solution." That is PAS 24 years before Kennedy's book, and Schwartz reserves it for one
awareness stage.

**Structure.** Name a problem the reader has, make it felt, present the fix.

**When it fits.** Problem-aware readers (Schwartz: has a need, does not connect it to a product). First DM. Not an
invitation note: there is no room to solve. Not an unaware reader: naming a problem they do not feel reads as
presumptuous.

**How to make it work on LinkedIn.** Their problem in their words (from their post or their role), one clause of
cost, then the fix with proof. The evidence (section 2) says spend words on efficacy, not on agitation.

**Example, invitation note.**
EN: "Claire, nine days of close mostly spent chasing invoices, as you wrote, is a common carrier problem and a
fixable one. I work on exactly that. Happy to connect." (160 characters; French 182)
FR : « Claire, neuf jours de clôture passés surtout à relancer des factures, comme vous l'écriviez : problème
fréquent chez les transporteurs, et soluble. C'est mon métier. Ravi d'échanger. »

**Example, first DM.**
EN: "Claire, you wrote that most of your nine-day close goes on chasing carrier and fuel invoices. That time usually
hides money too: duplicates and wrong surcharges that get paid because nobody can check every line. We check every
line before payment; a carrier your size found 41 such invoices in a quarter and now closes in six days. Want the
two-page summary?"
FR : « Claire, vous écriviez que l'essentiel de vos neuf jours de clôture part en relances de factures transport
et carburant. Ce temps cache souvent de l'argent : doublons et surcharges erronées payés faute de pouvoir tout
vérifier. Nous contrôlons chaque ligne avant paiement ; un transporteur de votre taille a trouvé 41 factures de ce
type en un trimestre et clôture désormais en six jours. Je vous envoie le résumé de deux pages ? »

**Evidence.** None for the formula. Agitation is the weak part (threat strength r = .10); efficacy is the strong
part (r = .198). Practice and survey sources warn that agitation reads as fear-mongering in a cold message
(`../cold-email/`).

### PASO (Problem, Agitate, Solve, Outcome)

**Origin.** Belinda Weaver, Copywrite Matters, 8 August 2019, presented as her addition to PAS (read). Other
variants listed by blogs: PASOC (adds a call to action), EPAS (empathy first). Untraced.

**Structure.** PAS plus the picture of life after the fix.

**When it fits.** Problem-aware readers where the outcome is concrete (a day saved, a number recovered). The
outcome step is the "visualization" of Monroe and the "after" of BAB, and it carries the efficacy that the
evidence rewards.

**Example, follow-up.**
EN: "Claire, picture the close at six days: invoices already checked when they reach your team, and the dispute
list ready for carriers on day one. That is what changed for the carrier I mentioned. Worth 15 minutes to see if
it holds for you? If not, no problem."
FR : « Claire, imaginez une clôture en six jours : des factures déjà vérifiées quand elles arrivent chez vous, et
la liste des litiges prête pour les transporteurs dès le premier jour. C'est ce qui a changé chez le transporteur
dont je vous parlais. Quinze minutes pour voir si cela tient chez vous ? Sinon, aucun souci. »

**Evidence.** None.

### PASTOR (Ray Edwards)

**Origin.** Ray Edwards, *How to Write Copy That Sells* (Morgan James, 2016) and, earlier, his blog post of 25 July 2014 (read in full on
Goodreads' mirror of his post). His own expansion: Problem; Amplify (the cost of not solving it, which he says is
"probably the most neglected step in the process"); Story and Solution (a true story of how it was solved); Transformation and Testimony (the
result, shown by real people); Offer (most of the space on the transformation, each deliverable tied back to it);
Response (exactly what to do next). The name is his: a pastor as a shepherd who guides rather than pushes, "I am not suggesting any
religious overtones" (his words). Several secondary sources wrongly expand T as only "Testimony".

**When it fits.** Sales pages and long emails. Six parts do not fit one LinkedIn message. Spread over a sequence:
message 1 Problem plus Amplify (one clause), message 2 Story and Transformation, message 3 Offer and Response.

**Example, follow-up (the "Story and Testimony" message of a sequence).**
EN: "Claire, the finance lead at the carrier I mentioned put it this way: 'We stopped arguing with suppliers from
memory; we argue from the list.' Their close went from nine days to six. I can send you the list format they use,
if it helps."
FR : « Claire, la directrice financière du transporteur dont je vous parlais le résume ainsi : "On ne discute plus
avec les fournisseurs de mémoire, on discute avec la liste." Leur clôture est passée de neuf à six jours. Je peux
vous envoyer le modèle de liste qu'ils utilisent, si cela vous aide. »
(The quote must be real and approved by the person quoted.)

**Evidence.** None.

---

## 6. The outcome family: BAB, FAB, the "So what?" test, 4Ps and PPPP, 4Us

### BAB (Before, After, Bridge)

**Origin.** No inventor or first use found in any source (Mailchimp, Campaign Monitor, GMass and Buffer describe
it without attribution). Untraced.

**Structure.** Their world now, their world with the problem solved, how to get from one to the other.

**When it fits.** Solution-aware readers (Schwartz: knows what they want, does not know a product does it) and
follow-ups that carry a customer result. Requires a real "after".

**Example, invitation note.**
EN: "Claire, from a nine-day close spent chasing invoices to six days with every line checked before payment: we
did that for a carrier your size. Glad to connect." (158 characters; French 163)
FR : « Claire, passer d'une clôture de neuf jours à six, chaque facture vérifiée avant paiement : nous l'avons
fait pour un transporteur de votre taille. Ravi d'échanger. »

**Example, first DM.**
EN: "Claire, today: nine days of close, most of it chasing invoices. A carrier your size is at six days now, with a
dispute list ready on day one. What got them there was checking every freight line against the rate card before
payment. Would it help to see how they set it up?"
FR : « Claire, aujourd'hui : neuf jours de clôture, surtout passés à relancer des factures. Un transporteur de
votre taille en est à six jours, avec la liste des litiges prête dès le premier jour. Ce qui a fait la différence :
contrôler chaque ligne de transport contre la grille avant paiement. Voulez-vous voir comment ils l'ont mis en
place ? »

**Evidence.** None. Vividness (r = .15) and efficacy (r = .198) are the measured ingredients a good "after"
supplies.

### FAB (Features, Advantages, Benefits) and the "So what?" test

**Origin.** Feature-advantage-benefit selling is sales-training folklore of unknown origin (a 1950s Xerox story
circulates; nothing confirms it). Neil Rackham's *SPIN Selling* (1988), from Huthwaite's study of about 35,000
sales calls over 12 years, is the only research on it (proprietary data, mostly 1970s and 1980s, never independently
replicated): in small sales, advantages beat bare features; in large
sales, features and advantages drew more objections, and only benefits defined as meeting a need the buyer had
explicitly stated went with success. Read through summaries and the book's table of contents ("The Relative
Impacts of Features, Advantages, and Benefits"), not the chapter itself.

The **"So what?" test** has no traceable coiner: after each claim, ask "so what?" as the reader would, and keep
going until the answer is something they feel in their week. It is the editing tool that turns a feature into a
benefit, and it is also the cure for the recited-fact failure (`../linkedin-messages/`, finding 1): "Ten years in
water network maintenance." fails the test at once.

**When it fits.** FAB fits a product-aware reader who asked "what exactly do you do?". Rackham's finding moves the
benefit from "what it does for anyone" to "what it does for the need they told you about": on LinkedIn, the need
in their own post.

**Example, reply to "what do you do exactly?" (a follow-up type).**
EN: "We check every freight invoice line against the rate card and the delivery record (feature), so errors are
caught before payment instead of in an audit months later (advantage). For you that means the invoice chasing you
said eats your close mostly disappears (benefit, tied to what you wrote)."
FR : « Nous vérifions chaque ligne de facture transport contre la grille tarifaire et le bon de livraison
(caractéristique), donc les erreurs sont repérées avant paiement et non lors d'un audit des mois plus tard
(avantage). Pour vous, les relances de factures qui, selon vous, mangent votre clôture disparaissent en grande
partie (bénéfice, lié à ce que vous avez écrit). »
(The labels in brackets are for the reader of this file, not for the message.)

**Evidence.** Rackham: measured (observational, his own firm's research, read through summaries). "So what?":
practice.

### 4Ps (Promise, Picture, Proof, Push) and PPPP (Picture, Promise, Prove, Push)

**Origin.** Untraced. One Goodreads reading note from a book by Michael Spitz attributes "Picture, Promise, Prove,
Push" to a "Henry" in the 1930s, read as Henry Hoke (direct mail publisher); the name is cut off. A reader's
highlight of Bob Bly's *The Copywriter's Handbook* lists "Picture, Promise, Prove, Push"; Bly's own book is better
known for his five-step "motivating sequence". AWAI, Copyblogger and GetResponse teach Promise, Picture, Proof,
Push without an author. Not to be confused with McCarthy's marketing mix (product, price, place, promotion).

**Structure.** A promise of a result, a picture of it, proof that it is real, a push to act.

**When it fits.** A message that carries a number or a case: first DM to a solution-aware reader, or a follow-up.
On LinkedIn cut it to Promise and Proof plus a soft Push.

**Example, first DM.**
EN: "Claire, three days off your close (promise). Your team opens invoices that are already checked, with the
disputes listed (picture). A 300-truck carrier went from nine days to six with us last quarter, numbers checked by
their controller (proof). Shall I send the two pages? (push)"
FR : « Claire, trois jours de moins sur votre clôture. Votre équipe ouvre des factures déjà vérifiées, litiges
listés. Un transporteur de 300 camions est passé de neuf à six jours avec nous le trimestre dernier, chiffres
vérifiés par son contrôleur. Je vous envoie les deux pages ? »

**Evidence.** None.

### 4Us (Urgent, Unique, Ultra-specific, Useful)

**Origin.** AWAI (American Writers and Artists Institute), June 2001: "Michael Masterson and Bill Bonner came up
with four ways to make your bullets stand out", "the Secret of the 4 U's" (read). Written for bullet points; now
taught for headlines and subject lines. One blog credits Bob Bly; unverified.

**Structure.** Rate a line on four qualities: a reason to act now, something only you can say, exact facts, a
benefit to the reader.

**When it fits.** As a test, not a template: the first line of a note, the first 40 or so characters a LinkedIn
inbox preview shows, a cold email subject. "Urgent" is the dangerous one in outreach: fake urgency is a sales
pressure tell and the opposite of the "free to say no" finding. Score Useful and Ultra-specific first.

**Example, a note's first line scored.**
EN, weak: "Quick question about your finance processes" (not specific, not useful, not unique).
EN, strong: "Claire, 41 wrong freight invoices in one quarter at a 300-truck carrier" (specific, useful, unique to
the sender; urgency left out on purpose).
FR, faible : « Petite question sur vos process finance »
FR, fort : « Claire, 41 factures transport erronées en un trimestre chez un transporteur de 300 camions »

**Evidence.** None for the formula. Ultra-specific is the part with evidence (section 9).

---

## 7. The guided-journey family: QUEST, SLAP, 1-2-3-4

### QUEST (Qualify, Understand, Educate, Stimulate, Transition)

**Origin, traced.** Michel Fortin, who says he created it in the late 1990s while teaching professional selling at
Algonquin College, as a memory aid, and expanded it in *The Death of the Salesletter* (2006). His own page (read):
Qualify, "make the right prospect feel seen fast"; Understand, "earn attention through credible empathy";
Educate, "introduce the solution without the offer"; Stimulate, "build desire and build value"; Transition, "one
clear next step, not several options". He frames it as an extension of AIDA: AIDA "fit an ad", QUEST "fit a full
salesletter". He notes that in B2B the Qualify stage is "almost always underinvested", and that an email sequence
can carry one or two stages per message. A different expansion (Question, Unpack, Emphasize, Solution, Transform)
circulates from an AI tool and is not his.

**When it fits.** A three-message LinkedIn sequence: note = Qualify; first DM = Understand plus Educate; follow-up =
Stimulate plus Transition. Its Qualify stage is the same move as Schwartz's identification headline and the
practitioners' "premise".

**Example, the three messages.**
Note EN: "Claire, finance leads at carriers who say close is mostly invoice chasing are the people I work with.
Happy to connect." (119 characters; French 147)
Note FR : « Claire, je travaille avec les directions financières de transporteurs pour qui la clôture, c'est surtout
des relances de factures. Ravi d'échanger. »
DM EN: "Thanks Claire. What you described, chasing carrier and fuel invoices, usually comes from checking by
sample: nobody can check every line by hand. Checking every line automatically against the rate card is what
changes it."
DM FR : « Merci Claire. Ce que vous décriviez, relancer les factures transport et carburant, vient souvent du
contrôle par sondage : personne ne peut tout vérifier à la main. Vérifier automatiquement chaque ligne contre la
grille, c'est ce qui change la donne. »
Follow-up EN: "A carrier your size closes in six days now, with 41 errors caught in a quarter. If it is useful, I can
run the same check on one month of your invoices. Free to say no."
Follow-up FR : « Un transporteur de votre taille clôture maintenant en six jours, avec 41 erreurs repérées en un
trimestre. Si c'est utile, je peux faire le même contrôle sur un mois de vos factures. Vous êtes libre de dire
non. »

**Evidence.** None.

### SLAP (Stop, Look, Act, Purchase)

**Origin.** Untraced; appears in 2010s copywriting lists (Swipefile, Mailchimp) described as a formula for
inexpensive products and social posts.

**When it fits.** It does not fit B2B outreach: "Purchase" in a first message is the meeting-first ask that the
outreach data shows performs worst (`../linkedin-messages/`). Listed here so nobody adopts it by mistake. No
example.

**Evidence.** None.

### The 1-2-3-4 formula

**Origin.** Untraced. The four prompts, "What I've got for you", "What it's going to do for you", "Who am I", "What
you need to do next", come from a Copyblogger article republished by Swipefile, with no author named. Often
attributed online to various copywriters; no attribution survived checking.

**When it fits.** Most-aware readers, who already want this kind of thing: a reply to someone who asked, an inbound
lead, a referral. It is product-first, which Schwartz says only works when the reader already knows they want it.

**Example, a reply to someone who commented "interested" on a post (first DM).**
EN: "Claire, here is the two-page audit summary you asked for (1). It shows where freight invoices leak money and
how a carrier your size took three days off its close (2). I'm Marc, I run the audit service behind it (3). If you
want, send me one month of invoices and I'll run the same check (4)."
FR : « Claire, voici le résumé d'audit de deux pages que vous demandiez (1). Il montre où les factures transport
font perdre de l'argent et comment un transporteur de votre taille a gagné trois jours de clôture (2). Je suis
Marc, je dirige le service d'audit derrière (3). Si vous le souhaitez, envoyez-moi un mois de factures et je fais
le même contrôle (4). »

**Evidence.** None.

---

## 8. The story family: Star-Story-Solution, Hook-Story-Offer

### Star-Story-Solution

**Origin.** Untraced. One Substack post (Start and Grow) says it was created by Vince James and adapted by Russell
Brunson in *DotCom Secrets*; no second source confirms it. GMass and Buffer describe it without attribution.

**Structure.** A star (a person like the reader), the story of their struggle and turn, the solution that worked,
then a call to action.

**When it fits.** A follow-up carrying a customer story, for problem- or solution-aware readers. On LinkedIn the
story is two sentences, not ten.

**Example, follow-up.**
EN: "Claire, the finance director at a 300-truck carrier had your exact nine-day close. She tried a second
accounts clerk; it moved one day. What moved three was checking every freight line before payment. Happy to
introduce you to her if a peer view helps."
FR : « Claire, la directrice financière d'un transporteur de 300 camions avait exactement votre clôture en neuf
jours. Elle a essayé un second comptable fournisseurs : un jour de gagné. Ce qui en a fait gagner trois, c'est le
contrôle de chaque ligne avant paiement. Je peux vous la présenter si l'avis d'une pair vous aide. »
(Only with her agreement.)

**Evidence.** Narrative vs non-narrative r = .067, statistical vs narrative evidence r = .044 (measured): a story
has, at most, a small edge over a plain statement of the same fact.

### Hook-Story-Offer (Russell Brunson)

**Origin.** Russell Brunson, *DotCom Secrets* (2015), *Expert Secrets* (2017), *Traffic Secrets* (2020; Penguin
Random House page read). He says that when a funnel underperforms the cause is always the hook, the story or the
offer (podcast summary). Read through publisher pages and summaries, not the books.

**Structure.** A hook that stops the scroll, a story that makes the reader believe, an offer that solves their
problem.

**When it fits.** LinkedIn posts and funnels more than private messages. In a DM the "hook" must be the
identification line, not a curiosity trick; a clickbait first line in a private message reads as a pitch.

**Example, a post-shaped first DM is not recommended; as a follow-up:**
EN: "Claire, 41 (hook). That's how many wrong freight invoices a carrier your size paid in one quarter before they
checked every line; their controller found them in a week (story). I can run the same check on one month of your
invoices, free (offer)."
FR : « Claire, 41. C'est le nombre de factures transport erronées qu'un transporteur de votre taille a payées en
un trimestre avant de tout vérifier ; son contrôleur les a retrouvées en une semaine. Je peux faire le même
contrôle sur un mois de vos factures, gratuitement. »

**Evidence.** None published; Brunson's results are his own businesses (vendor).

---

## 9. The masters: Schwartz, Caples, Ogilvy

### Eugene Schwartz, the five states of awareness (Breakthrough Advertising, 1966, chapter 2, read in full)

**Correction to `../personas/README.md`:** that file says no page quotes Schwartz's own wording and the five labels
may be a modern compilation. The book's text was read for this pass. The five stages are his, under different names
from the modern shorthand:

| Schwartz's own heading | Modern shorthand | What he says the headline does |
|---|---|---|
| 1. The Most Aware: "knows of your product, knows what it does, knows he wants it" | Most aware | Name of product and price; "there is nothing creative about his job" |
| 2. The Customer Knows of the Product But Doesn't Yet Want It | Product aware | Name the product and point out its superiority; reinforce desire, sharpen the image, extend it, introduce a new mechanism |
| 3. How to Introduce New Products: "knows he wants what the product does; but he doesn't yet know that there is a product" | Solution aware | Start with the desire, then the product |
| 4. How to Introduce Products That Solve Needs: "has a need... doesn't yet realize the connection" | Problem aware | Name the need, dramatize it, present the product as "the inevitable solution" (that is PAS) |
| 5. How to Open Up a Completely Unaware Market | Unaware | No price, no product, no function, no desire: "Your market, of course!"; an "identification headline" that echoes "an emotion, an attitude, a dissatisfaction"; its only job is to get the next paragraph read |

He also says "each of these stages is separated from the others by a psychological wall": a headline that works at
one stage "will fail completely" at another.

**For LinkedIn.** A cold invitation goes to someone who does not know you exist: stages 4 and 5. So the note and
the first line of a DM should be identification (who they are, what they said, what they live), not product. The
product appears only when the reader has moved, which on LinkedIn means after they replied or engaged.

**Examples, a stage-5 identification note.**
EN: "Claire, your line about spending close chasing invoices instead of reading the numbers stayed with me. Many
finance leads in transport say the same. Glad to connect." (165 characters; French 197)
FR : « Claire, votre phrase sur la clôture passée à relancer des factures plutôt qu'à lire les chiffres m'est
restée. Beaucoup de directions financières du transport disent la même chose. Ravi d'échanger. »

### Schwartz, the five stages of market sophistication (chapter 3, read in full)

His third question before any headline: "How many similar products have they been told about before?"

1. **First in the market:** "Be simple. Be direct." Name the need or the claim; prove it works.
2. **Second:** if the direct claim still works, "copy that successful claim, but enlarge on it".
3. **Third:** prospects "have now heard all the claims"; shift from what the product does to "HOW it works": the
   mechanism.
4. **Fourth:** enlarge the mechanism (easier, quicker, surer).
5. **Fifth:** "your market no longer believes in your advertising"; "the emphasis shifts from the promise and the
   mechanism... to identification with the prospect himself".

**For LinkedIn.** Treat most B2B services sold by cold message as stage five: the reader has seen every claim and
every "AI-powered" mechanism. Use identification first. A genuinely new mechanism (stage three) can work if it is
real and checkable ("we check every line against the rate card" is a mechanism; "our AI optimizes your finance" is
not). Claim inflation (stage two) reads as spam.

**Evidence.** Practice. Schwartz built it on decades of mail-order results he does not publish in the book.

### John Caples, Tested Advertising Methods (1932; fifth edition revised by Fred E. Hahn, 1997, read)

**What matters for messages.**
- **Testing as the method.** Caples' method is keyed coupons: every ad carries a code, so each version's
  responses are counted. His rules come from those counts; most of the counts are reported as stories, not
  tables. Rating: practice with counts.
- **Specific versus general.** The used car dealer story ("Better automobile values" flopped; ads naming make,
  year and price drew "three times as many customers" by actual count). And: "the statement that '97,482 people
  have bought one of these appliances' is stronger than the statement 'Nearly 100,000 of these appliances have
  been sold.' The first statement sounds like a fact." He adds the reason most copy stays general: "it requires
  time and trouble to collect specific data." The same is true of a LinkedIn message.
- **Self-interest or news.** His headline rule, repeated by Ogilvy: the best headlines "appeal to the reader's
  self-interest or give news". On LinkedIn: their situation or something new to them, never "I wanted to reach
  out".
- **Address a specific person or group** (his rule 33) and **ask a question** (rule 34) are listed as headline
  types that worked in his tests. The measured average effect of rhetorical questions is small (r = .059).

### David Ogilvy

**Read:** his foreword to Caples' fourth edition, reprinted in the fifth. He lists what Caples taught him,
including "What you say is more important than how you say it", "The most effective headlines appeal to the
reader's self-interest or give news", "Specifics are more believable than generalities", and calls Caples a man
with "no theories; only facts". **Not read, secondary:** "The more informative your advertising, the more
persuasive it will be" is widely attributed to Ogilvy (*Confessions of an Advertising Man*, 1963, per a reader's
claim; the book is lending-only on the Internet Archive). His Rolls-Royce headline ("At 60 miles an hour the
loudest noise in this new Rolls-Royce comes from the electric clock") is the canonical specific claim; he took the
fact from a technical editor's road test, and one secondary source says a Pierce-Arrow ad used a similar line
decades earlier (unverified).

**For LinkedIn.** One exact fact the reader can check beats three adjectives. "Specific" also covers the ask:
"Shall I send the two-page summary?" beats "Let me know if you'd like to chat."

**Evidence for specificity beyond the masters.** Precise numbers are read as coming from a more confident and
knowledgeable source (Jerez-Fernandez, Angulo and Oppenheimer, "Show me the numbers", Psychological Science 25(2), 633-635, 2014;
bibliographic record only, no abstract read). Schindler and
Yalch (Advances in Consumer Research 33, 2006) studied whether sharp numbers in ad claims are believed more
(abstract only). Specific recommendation vs general r = .10 and vividness r = .15 (O'Keefe and Hoeken, measured).

---

## 10. Decision table: message type x awareness level -> framework

Awareness uses Schwartz's stages (section 9). On LinkedIn, the first contact is almost always stage 4 or 5; a reply,
a comment on your post or an inbound request moves the reader to 2 or 1.

| Message type | 5. Unaware | 4. Problem aware (need) | 3. Solution aware (desire) | 2. Product aware | 1. Most aware |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Invitation note (200 chars) | Schwartz identification, or QUEST Qualify | One-clause PAS (problem + "fixable") | One-line BAB | Specific proof line (4Us check) | Skip the note's pitch: a plain "as discussed" |
| First DM after acceptance | Identification + one question about their situation (no product) | PAS with one clause of agitation, or PASO | BAB, or 4Ps cut to Promise + Proof | FAB through the "So what?" test, AIDCA proof | 1-2-3-4 |
| Follow-up 1 (new value) | Star-Story-Solution about someone like them | PASO outcome, or Star-Story-Solution | Proof message (AIDCA conviction) | Proof or mechanism (Schwartz stage 3) | Offer with a specific next step |
| Follow-up 2 / breakup | One-line "free to say no" close | Same | Same | Same | Same |
| Reply to an inbound or an engager | (not applicable) | ACCA comprehension line + offer | BAB | FAB | 1-2-3-4 |
| A post (not a DM) | Hook-Story-Offer with an identification hook | Hook-Story-Offer, PAS | BAB | Proof | Offer |

Across every cell: one exact fact about them, one exact proof, one exact and easy next step, the exit offered
(section 1). Sophistication overlay: when the reader's market is crowded with similar offers (most B2B), move one
column to the left in what the opening may claim.

---

## 11. What was corrected or added

| Where | Said | Now |
|---|---|---|
| `../personas/README.md`, Schwartz | "No page reached quotes Schwartz's own wording"; labels may be compiled | Book read: five stages are his, with the headings in section 9; the modern labels are shorthand for them |
| `../cold-email/README.md`, PAS | "Classic direct-response copy formula, no traceable inventor" | Still no inventor; Schwartz (1966) gives the same recipe for his stage 4, and Kennedy (1990) popularised the name |
| `../linkedin-messages/README.md`, 4Ps | "4Ps (Hoke, untraced)" | Still untraced; two orderings exist, the Hoke attribution rests on one cut-off book note |
| Common claim | "AIDA, Lewis, 1898" | Disputed by Iwamoto (2024); acronym by C. P. Russell (1921); Sheldon added satisfaction (1911); Dukesmith had conviction (1904) |
| Common claim | "PASTOR: Problem, Amplify, Story, Testimony, Offer, Response" | Edwards' own text: Story and Solution, Transformation and Testimony |
| Common claim | "This framework converts better" | The one controlled test of an order found no difference; single design choices average r = .10 and can flip |

---

## 12. Open questions

- No study compares two copy frameworks on LinkedIn messages or cold email. BeReach's own `bereach_status`
  (replies to first messages within 7 days) could run that test: same list split, same facts, two shapes.
- Schwartz's stages were built on mass-market mail order; whether a B2B reader's awareness can be read off a
  profile and a post is untested.
- The "but you are free" effect shrinks in the best-designed studies; whether it survives in a cold B2B message is
  unknown.
